entries.seminar_title: Climate, Biodiversity, and Environmental Damage: Evidence from Oceans and Railroads
entries.speaker: Seung Min Kim
entries.abstract: Climate change and biodiversity loss are the "twin crises" of the Anthropocene, yet little causal evidence exists on how they interact. We ask whether biodiversity loss amplifies the effect of climate on wildfire risk in western U.S. forests. We exploit nineteenth-century railroad land grants, whose zones were fixed by statute before systematic vegetation surveys and whose checkerboarded parcels were largely clear-cut. Comparing firesheds almost fully covered by grant zones with their neighbors, we find that railroad exposure reduced old-growth forest (a proxy for tree diversity) and increased checkerboarding by 35% and 38% of a standard deviation, respectively. To address endogenous local climate, we instrument seasonal vapor pressure deficit with shift-share instruments built from Pacific Decadal Variability, using fireshed-specific teleconnection weights estimated on 1895–1980 data. In a 1985–2024 fireshed-year panel, large-fire occurrence in high-exposure firesheds is roughly four times as sensitive to drought as in low-exposure firesheds. The gap stems mainly from cool-season dryness, which ordinarily curbs fire by limiting fuel growth but offers less protection in railroad-exposed landscapes. The gap is starkest for high-severity fires. The results reveal an unintended, long-lived cost of infrastructure development, operating through the destruction of nonrenewable natural capital. They also suggest that climate damages depend on the state of ecosystems.
